messages.text: Hey Priya! You look worried today. What's going on?

options.text: I have no money left and it's only the 20th!
Just tired, nothing serious

messages.text: Oh no! That happens to me too sometimes. Do you know where it all went?
Are you sure? You've been quiet all day... Is it money problems again?
Do you actually track what you spend?

options.text: No, I just buy what we need
I try to remember but always forget

messages.text: That's exactly the problem! If you don't write it down, it just disappears.
Remembering doesn't work — trust me, I tried that for years.
Here, I saw this the other day and it really stuck with me...
Most families don't know where 30% of their money goes each month. Writing it down changes everything.
So let's try together right now. How much did Raj bring home this month?

options.text: Around 8,000 Rs
I'm not sure exactly...

messages.text: Perfect! That's your income. Now let's see where it went.
That's okay — even a rough number is a good start. Let's say around 8,000.
Now think — rent, food, transport... Add it all up. What did you spend?

options.text: About 5,500 Rs I think
I really don't know...

messages.text: So you still have 2,500 Rs left! See — you do know your money.
Let's estimate. Rent 2,000, food 3,000, transport 500 — that's already 5,500. So you have 2,500 left!
Income − Expenses = What's left. 8,000 − 5,500 = 2,500 Rs. This number is called your balance.
You just did your first expense check! That wasn't so hard, was it?

options.text: I can't believe I never did this before!
It feels overwhelming though...

messages.text: Now imagine doing this every month. Everything becomes clearer!
I know that feeling. But the first time is always the hardest. It gets easier, I promise.
Priya, I heard you girls talking. Can I share something?
Of course, Meena!
For years I had no idea where our money went. One day I just started writing everything down in a notebook. Within one month — I found 800 Rs we were wasting without even knowing.
The first step to controlling your money is simply knowing where it goes. You cannot change what you don't measure.
Start today. Even a small notebook works. Your future self will thank you.
Priya! Raj got his salary today, right? How are you feeling about this month?

options.text: Hopeful! I want to track everything this time
Nervous... we always seem to run short

messages.text: I love that attitude! Let's do this properly together.
I understand. But that's exactly why we're doing this — no more surprises at the end of the month.
First question — do you know exactly how much Raj earned this month?

options.text: Yes — 10,000 Rs
He mentioned a number but I forgot...

messages.text: Great! Write that down. That's your income.
Go ask him tonight — you need to know this number. It's the foundation of everything.
Income = all the money that comes INTO your household each month. Salary, extra work, any other source. Know this number first — always.
Now the other side — what did the family spend this month?

options.text: Rent 2,000, food 3,000, transport 500... maybe 2,000 more on other things
I didn't track it properly this time

messages.text: So that's 7,500 Rs total. Let's see what's left!
Let's estimate together. Rent? Food? Transport? Even rough numbers tell us a lot.
Expenses = all the money that goes OUT of your household each month. Big ones: rent, food, school fees, medicine. Small ones add up too — chai, auto, snacks.
So — 10,000 in, 7,500 out. What does that leave?

options.text: I'm not sure, I'm bad at maths...

messages.text: Exactly! That's your balance. That's what you have left to work with.
10,000 minus 7,500 equals 2,500. That's your balance — what's left after all expenses.
Income − Expenses = Balance. 10,000 − 7,500 = 2,500 Rs. If balance is POSITIVE → you're okay. If balance is NEGATIVE → you're spending more than you earn. This leads to debt.

options.text: 2,500 is not bad actually!
What if the balance is negative though?

messages.text: Right! And now you can decide what to do with those 2,500 Rs instead of just watching them disappear.
Great question. That's when you need to look at your expenses and find what can be reduced. We'll talk about that soon.
Girls, may I say something?
Please, Meena!
When my husband and I first wrote down our income and expenses — we discovered we were spending 1,200 Rs a month on things we couldn't even remember buying.

options.text: 1,200 Rs! That's so much...
How did you even find that out?

messages.text: Exactly. Small purchases every day add up to a big number by the end of the month.
We just wrote everything down for one month. Every single purchase. The number shocked us both.
One simple habit: At the end of each day, write down everything you spent. After one month, you will see your true spending picture clearly.
Knowing your numbers is not about being perfect. It's about being aware. Awareness is where change begins.
Priya, you've been tracking your expenses for a few weeks now. How does it feel?

options.text: So much better! I finally know where my money goes
It's helpful but I still feel like I'm not in control

messages.text: That's exactly how it should feel! Now I want to show you the next step.
Tracking is just the first step. What I'm about to show you will give you real control.
Have you ever heard of a budget?

options.text: Isn't that something only rich people do?
I've heard the word but don't really know what it means

messages.text: That's what I thought too! But actually it's the opposite — it's how ordinary people stop feeling poor.
It's simpler than it sounds, I promise. Let me explain.
A budget means you DECIDE in advance where each rupee will go — before the month even starts.
A budget is a plan for your money. Instead of wondering where it went — you tell it where to go. You are in control, not your money.

options.text: So I plan everything at the start of the month?
But what if something unexpected happens?

messages.text: Exactly! You sit down, look at your income, and decide: this much for food, this much for rent, this much to save.
Such a good question! That's why a budget always includes a small amount for surprises. We never know everything that will happen.
I used to feel guilty every time I spent money. Like I was doing something wrong.

options.text: Yes! I feel that way all the time
Really? But you always seem so confident

messages.text: A budget changed that for me. When you planned to spend it — there's no guilt. It's allowed.
Ha! It took me a long time to get here. A budget gave me that confidence.
A budget is not a restriction. It's permission to spend — without guilt. When you planned it, you earned the right to spend it.
Priya, I want to tell you something that happened in our home.
Please tell us, Meena!
Twenty years ago, my husband and I fought about money every single week. We never had enough, always blamed each other.

options.text: That sounds so stressful...
Raj and I argue about money too sometimes

messages.text: It was. Until one day a neighbour showed us how to make a simple plan together. Our first budget.
Most couples do, dear. Money is the number one cause of family arguments. But a budget changes that.
When you both agree on the plan before the month starts — there is nothing to argue about. The plan decides, not the emotions.
Families with a budget argue about money significantly less than those without one. A shared plan creates shared understanding.
So Priya — are you ready to make your very first budget?

options.text: Yes! I actually feel excited about this
A little nervous, but yes — let's do it

messages.text: Let's go! Your budget is waiting.
That nervousness means you care. And that's enough to start.
You just unlocked your Budget tab! Enter your monthly income and start planning where your money goes. Your first budget starts now.
Priya! You look stressed again. What happened?

options.text: I have no money left but I don't know why...
I spent too much this month but I'm not sure where

messages.text: That is exactly what happened to me last year. Let me show you something important.
I know that feeling. Money just seems to disappear, right? Let me help you understand why.
Tell me — what did you buy this month?

options.text: Food, rent, school fees... and some new clothes
Medicines, electricity bill... and some snacks and things for the house

messages.text: Good. Now — which of those could you NOT skip?
Okay. Now think — which of those were absolutely necessary?
There are two types of expenses, Priya. Things you NEED and things you WANT.

NEEDS — Must pay every month: Food and ration, Rent or house payment, Children's school fees, Medicines and health costs, Electricity and water bill, SHG savings contribution. WANTS — Extra spending: Extra snacks or sweets, New clothes outside festivals, Entertainment, Gifts beyond budget.
Your needs must always come first. Always. No matter what.

options.text: But sometimes I buy wants without thinking...
I always pay rent and food first, but the rest gets mixed up

messages.text: That is normal! We all do it. The trick is to know the difference BEFORE you spend.
That is a good start! But we need to make sure ALL needs are paid before any wants.
Radha earns ₹7,000 this month. School fees and ration → NEED ✓. New saree → WANT. Extra sweets → WANT. Mobile recharge → WANT. Needs always come before wants. Radha pays school fees and ration FIRST.
Think about last month. What did you buy that was a want — not a need?

options.text: I bought new bangles... but we needed medicine money too
I bought extra snacks for the children... but rent was still due

messages.text: Exactly. If you had listed your needs first, you would have seen there was not enough left for bangles.
Yes! The snacks felt small. But small wants add up and steal from your needs.
Girls, can I share something?
Please, Meena!
When my children were young, I bought sweets and small things without thinking. By the 20th — no money for school fees.

options.text: That is exactly my situation, Meena!
How did you fix it?

messages.text: Then this lesson is exactly what you need, dear. You are not alone.
I started writing my needs first, before I went to the market. Everything changed after that.
The rule is simple: Write down ALL your needs first. Pay them ALL before buying any wants. What is left — that is your wants money.
Give your needs a name before your money leaves your hand. That is the only way.
Priya! It is the 1st of the month. Did Raj bring home the money?

options.text: Yes! He brought ₹8,000 this month
Only ₹6,000 this month — less work available

messages.text: Good month! Before you go to the market — sit with me for 10 minutes.
A harder month. That is okay. We will work with what we have. Sit with me first.
Before you spend a single rupee — tell me. What MUST you pay this month, no matter what?

options.text: Rent, school fees, ration, electricity... and my SHG amount
I'm not sure... rent and food I think?

messages.text: Perfect! You already know your list. Now write it down — before anything else.
Let us think together. Rent? School fees? Food? Medicine? SHG savings? Write each one down.
That list — those are your needs. That is your First List.
The First List is your money's to-do list. Write it on the 1st of every month — before chai, before market, before anything. Give every rupee a job before it leaves your hand.
Once you know what must go — you can see exactly what is left for everything else.

options.text: So I write needs first and only then think about wants?
What if there is not enough even for needs?

messages.text: Exactly! Needs first, always. What remains — that is your wants money. Not before.
In a hard month — focus only on the most critical needs. Food, medicines, school fees. Everything else waits.
In a good month: pay all needs, save a little extra for your emergency jar. In a low month: food, medicines, school fees come first — everything else waits. Always save something — even ₹50 counts.
Priya, I want to tell you something.
Tell us, Meena!
For years I could not understand where our money went. Then I started writing the First List on the 1st morning itself. Before chai. Before market. It changed everything.

options.text: Just writing it down made a difference?
I want to try this from tomorrow!

messages.text: Yes! When you write it, you see it clearly. You cannot pretend the rent does not exist when it is written in front of you.
Not tomorrow — today! It is the 1st. Write your First List right now, in the app.
Your money does not disappear. It goes to places you did not plan. A First List gives every rupee a name before it leaves your hand.
Start today. Even on paper. Even in your mind. The First List is the beginning of control.
